Wally Banes (4:45 P.M.)
Did you guys catch what Professor Lane said about the idea of the tragic
flaw in Aristotle’s Poetics? I’m still a bit confused.
Anita Verenne (4:47 P.M.)
Yeah, the key point was that it’s not a moral weakness—it’s a mistake or
limitation tied to the hero’s character.
Wally Banes (4:48 P.M.)
I was puzzled... the flaw can be admirable yet lead to a downfall?
Anita Verenne (4:50 P.M.)
Aristotle calls it hamartia—a misjudgment, not evil intent. Oedipus, for
example, is tragic because his determination to uncover the truth shows
courage, but it blinds him to warnings and drives him toward disaster.
Dong-woo Namgung (4:51 P.M.)
Professor Lane also noted that Oedipus in Sophocles’ play is arrogant
and quick to anger, but these traits weren’t “evil” for the ancient Greeks.
Wally Banes (4:52 P.M.)
Wow, this is so different from what I learned about the tragic flaw when I
studied it in high school!
Dong-woo Namgung (4:53 P.M.)
Yeah, Professor Lane said it’s hard for us to let go of moralizing when
we read literature.
